To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensitivity of cluster number count studies to the properties of dark energy is matched by an equally important sensitivity to the properties of cluster mass distributions and that this sensitivity can be used to internally calibrate cluster number counts and thereby improve dark energy constraints by a factor of $\ensuremath{>}$2.

cluster dark energy studies are sensitive to both the mean and the scatter of the observable-math proxy given the true mass, and that the shape of the distribution may provide internal consistency checks that will protect against incorrect dark energy interpretations.

(1) the observable-mass function is sensitive to the scatter of the observable-math distribution, (2) this can be self-calibrated by the observable-mass-function, (3) external constraints on the mass-variance of the distribution improve constraints on the equation of state by a factor of 1-2, and (4) the observable-math function provides internal checks on the assumed observable-math relation
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the dark energy using the abundance of galaxy clusters.
the development of methods to improve the accuracy of dark energy constraints using cluster counts, and to identify potential systematic errors.
the study of the dark energy using the cluster abundance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a measurement of the mass variance of a mass proxy to $\ensuremath{\lesssim}0.1$ at $z<1$ is required for the SPT survey to achieve a measurement of the equation of state of dark energy to $\ensuremath{w}_{0}\sim0.1$ and $\ensuremath{c}_{w}\sim0.3$.
the observable-mass distributions of clusters can be self-calibrated, but only if the scatter is small and the external constraints on the mass distribution are accurate.

the dark energy equation-of-state parameter $w$ may be determined to $\ensuremath{\delta}w\ensuremath{\simeq}0.2$ by the SPT survey if the mass distribution is well understood and the mass variance is known to within a few percent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a self-calibrating observable is a necessary condition for a self-calibratable dark energy measurement.
the number counts are a sensitive function of the properties of the mass distribution and the mass distribution itself is a sensitive function of dark energy.
cluster counts are not only an excellent tool for measuring dark energy, but also an excellent tool for studying the distribution of the observable-masses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the observable-mass proxy must be calibrated with exquisite precision to avoid a severe degradation of constraints on dark energy.
a careful study of the shape of the mass function and its observable proxy is essential to the success of cluster counts as dark energy probes.
cluster number counts are not only a probe of the dark energy, they are also a probe of the mass function of the cluster population.
